title: Bangladesh Deploys Paramilitary Troops as Unrest Grows Over Hasina's Planned Return
summary: Bangladesh has deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops nationwide after ten days of bomb blasts and arson attacks linked to former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's plan to return from exile in December, as her banned Awami League party calls a nationwide lockdown for November 19.
content:
Bangladesh has deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops across the country after ten days of bomb blasts, arson attacks and street clashes linked to former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's plan to return from exile in December, [according to Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/bangladesh-deploys-paramilitary-unrest-grows-over-hasinas-return-2026-11-18/). The security operation, launched on Wednesday, comes as her banned Awami League party builds toward a nationwide lockdown called for Thursday, November 19.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being torched in at least 28 districts over the last ten days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media reported. Dhaka Metropolitan Police arrested at least 71 members of banned organisations, including the Awami League and its affiliated outfits, in the last 24 hours alone, police spokesperson Niaz Mehedi said.

The unrest has been sharpest in Gopalganj, Hasina's hometown and an Awami League stronghold, where supporters staged violent demonstrations on Sunday, attacking police vehicles and installations and demanding her return from India. Authorities called out platoons of the paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh to stand alongside riot police in the district, and officials said deployments would be increased depending on how the situation develops.

Hasina, 79, has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka in August 2024, when a student-led uprising toppled her government after weeks of violent protests demanding her resignation. She has requested a new passport and identity card, saying she plans to return to Bangladesh in December. The interim government has so far rejected her request, and her supporters have taken to the streets since that refusal became clear.

Last week the Awami League announced a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Hasina's return, culminating in the nationwide lockdown on November 19. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said law enforcement agencies were determined to prevent sabotage and terrorism, and security forces have been placed on heightened alert in Dhaka and other major cities.

Tuesday also marked one year since Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal, which found her guilty of crimes against humanity over her government's crackdown on the 2024 uprising. She has repeatedly said since July that she intends to return to Bangladesh in December and face the legal proceedings against her, despite the death sentence.

The standoff leaves the interim government, led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, facing its most serious test since it took power after Hasina's fall. The Awami League, the party that led Bangladesh to independence and dominated its politics for a decade and a half under Hasina, is now banned from political activity, and its leaders are either in exile, in hiding or in custody. Yet the past ten days have shown it can still mobilise supporters willing to take to the streets, and the lockdown called for Thursday will be the clearest measure yet of how much street power it retains.

For Hasina herself, the practical obstacles to a return remain formidable. She has no valid Bangladeshi passport, the government has refused to issue her one, and she faces a death sentence the moment she sets foot in the country. Her supporters present her planned return as an act of defiance; her opponents call it a provocation designed to destabilise a country preparing for elections. Either way, the decision of whether, and how, she travels will fall largely on India, where she has sheltered for more than two years, and New Delhi has said little in public about her plans.

What happens on Thursday will shape what comes next. If the lockdown brings Bangladesh to a standstill, the interim government will face pressure to respond with still heavier security measures, deepening a confrontation it has tried to contain. If the streets stay quiet, it will suggest the Awami League's capacity to disrupt has been blunted by arrests and the ban. Beyond the immediate crisis, the episode has exposed a question Bangladesh has not yet answered: what place, if any, remains in its politics for the party that governed it for fifteen years, and for the leader it drove into exile.
